CHAPTER 26 — समसामयिकं संस्कृतसाहित्यम् (SAMSAMAYIKAM SANSKRITA-SAHITYAM)

Introduction — संस्कृतं जीवद्भाषा अस्ति (Sanskrit is a living language)

Many people wrongly believe that Sanskrit is a 'dead' language — a language of old books only, in which nothing new is ever written. This chapter shows the opposite. समसामयिकम् (sama-samayikam) means 'contemporary, belonging to the present time'. समसामयिकं संस्कृतसाहित्यम् therefore means the Sanskrit literature that is being composed TODAY — poems, songs, plays, novels, short stories, essays and even daily newspapers. अद्यापि संस्कृतेन नूतनानि काव्यानि, नाटकानि, कथाः, उपन्यासाः, पत्राणि च लिख्यन्ते। Even today new poems, plays, stories, novels and newspapers are written in Sanskrit. A language in which new literature is continuously born, in which news is read on the radio, in which children speak in some villages, is by definition a जीवद्भाषा — a living language.

अविच्छिन्ना परम्परा — An unbroken tradition

Sanskrit literature has flowed like a great river from the Vedas, through the Ramayana and Mahabharata, through the classical age of Kalidasa, Bhasa, Banabhatta and Bhavabhuti, into the medieval period — and that river has never stopped. In the nineteenth, twentieth and twenty-first centuries, hundreds of writers have continued to compose in every classical genre: महाकाव्यम् (the long epic poem), खण्डकाव्यम् (the shorter narrative poem), गीतकाव्यम् (lyric poetry and songs), नाटकम् (drama), and गद्यम् (prose). What has changed is not the language but the subject matter: modern Sanskrit writers sing of the nation and its freedom struggle, of nature and the environment, of science, of social reform, of the daily life of farmers, students and teachers. संस्कृतकवयः अधुना देशभक्तिं, प्रकृतिं, विज्ञानं, समाजजीवनं च वर्णयन्ति।

आधुनिकं पद्यसाहित्यम् — Modern Sanskrit poetry

गीतकाव्यम् (lyric poetry) is perhaps the most popular form of contemporary Sanskrit composition. Modern Sanskrit गीतानि (songs) are written for singing — patriotic songs (देशभक्तिगीतानि), prayer songs, songs on the seasons and on social themes — and are sung in schools, in Sanskrit camps and on Sanskrit Day. Traditional metres (छन्दांसि) such as अनुष्टुभ् are still used, but poets also compose in newer song-forms with refrains, so that even beginners can sing along.

The महाकाव्य (epic) tradition also continues. It is a remarkable fact that full-scale Sanskrit mahakavyas — long poems in many cantos (सर्गाः) on the lives of great men and women — have been composed in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. The contemporary scholar-poet Jagadguru Rambhadracharya, for example, has composed modern Sanskrit mahakavyas in recent decades, showing that the art of Valmiki and Kalidasa is still practised. Eminent twentieth-century scholars such as V. Raghavan of Madras not only studied classical literature deeply but also wrote and actively promoted new Sanskrit compositions, including plays and songs, proving by example that Sanskrit can carry modern thought.

कथासाहित्यम् — Novels and short stories

Sanskrit has an ancient and world-famous story tradition — the पञ्चतन्त्रम् and the हितोपदेशः travelled across the world in translation. Modern writers have carried this tradition forward into two newer forms: the उपन्यासः (novel) and the लघुकथा (short story). Contemporary Sanskrit short stories describe the everyday world around us — a farmer worried about the rains, a student preparing for an examination, a mother in a village, questions of honesty, poverty and kindness. The style is deliberately simple (सरला भाषा), close to spoken Sanskrit, so that ordinary readers can enjoy it. Novels and story collections appear from Sanskrit publishing houses, and many stories are first printed in Sanskrit magazines (पत्रिकाः). This growth of modern prose fiction is important evidence that Sanskrit is not confined to verse or to religious subjects: it can tell the story of today's society in today's settings.

नाटकम् — Modern Sanskrit drama

The drama (नाटकम्, more generally रूपकम्) has always been called the most delightful form of literature — काव्येषु नाटकं रम्यम्। Modern Sanskrit playwrights continue the tradition of Bhasa and Kalidasa, but their plays often deal with contemporary themes: social problems, national heroes, school life, even humorous sketches about modern gadgets. Short, simple plays in conversational Sanskrit are staged by students at school functions, university youth festivals and Sanskrit Day celebrations. The radio has created a new dramatic form, the श्रव्यनाटकम् (audio play / radio play), broadcast on आकाशवाणी (All India Radio). Drama is especially valuable for the Sanskrit movement because the audience HEARS living, spoken Sanskrit — dialogue (संवादः) brings the language off the page and onto the tongue.

संस्कृतपत्रकारिता — Sanskrit journalism

Perhaps the most striking proof that Sanskrit is alive is Sanskrit journalism (पत्रकारिता). The best-known example is सुधर्मा (Sudharma), a Sanskrit daily newspaper (दैनिकपत्रम्) published from Mysuru (Mysore) in Karnataka since 1970 — for over half a century it has reported politics, sport, science and world news entirely in Sanskrit. Besides Sudharma, a number of Sanskrit magazines and journals (पत्रिकाः) are published from different parts of India, carrying poems, stories, essays and news. आकाशवाणी (All India Radio) broadcasts daily Sanskrit news bulletins, and दूरदर्शनम् (Doordarshan television) has telecast Sanskrit news as well. On the अन्तर्जालम् (internet) one finds Sanskrit websites, blogs, e-magazines and video channels. To report a cricket match or a space launch in Sanskrit, journalists must constantly coin and use new words — and this daily exercise keeps the language supple and current.

संस्थाः पुरस्काराश्च — Institutions and awards

Modern Sanskrit literature is supported by institutions. The साहित्य-अकादमी (Sahitya Akademi), India's national academy of letters, has been giving its annual award for outstanding literary works since 1956, and Sanskrit is among the languages honoured — modern Sanskrit poets and prose writers have received this national recognition, which encourages new writing. Sanskrit universities and academies across India teach, publish and give prizes for new compositions. The organisation संस्कृतभारती (Samskrita Bharati) has spread spoken Sanskrit through thousands of सम्भाषणशिबिराणि (spoken-Sanskrit camps), teaching lakhs of people to converse in simple Sanskrit. In the village of Mattur (मत्तूरु) in Karnataka, Sanskrit is famously used in daily conversation. Sanskrit is one of the 22 languages listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution, and संस्कृतदिनम् (Sanskrit Day) is celebrated every year on श्रावणपूर्णिमा, with the surrounding week observed as Sanskrit Week in schools and colleges.

छात्राः किं कुर्युः? — How can students engage with living Sanskrit?

A senior-secondary student can take part in this living tradition in many simple ways: (1) पठनम् — read a Sanskrit magazine, a page of Sudharma, or simple modern stories; (2) श्रवणम् — listen to the Sanskrit news bulletin on radio or Sanskrit videos on the internet; (3) सम्भाषणम् — attend a spoken-Sanskrit camp and practise simple sentences daily (भवान् कथम् अस्ति? — How are you?); (4) लेखनम् — keep a short Sanskrit diary, write small verses or a letter to a friend; (5) अभिनयः — act in a short Sanskrit play on Sanskrit Day; (6) participate in recitation, quiz and essay competitions. Living languages live in the mouths and pens of the young.

व्याकरणम् — Grammar from the chapter

(A) सन्धिः: Contemporary prose uses the same sandhi rules as classical Sanskrit. Examples from this lesson: विद्या + आलयः → विद्यालयः (आ + आ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धिः, 'school'); अद्य + अपि → अद्यापि (अ + अ = आ, 'even today'); सम + समयः → belonging to the same समय gives समसामयिकम् 'contemporary'; च + एव → चैव; न + अस्ति → नास्ति। Splitting such forms back (सन्धि-विच्छेदः) remains a key reading skill, e.g. संस्कृतमस्ति = संस्कृतम् + अस्ति।

(B) समासः: Many modern coinages are compounds (समस्तपदानि). दूरदर्शनम् = दूरात् दर्शनम् ('seeing from afar' = television); दूरवाणी = दूरात् वाणी ('voice from afar' = telephone); अन्तर्जालम् = अन्तः जालम् ('inner net' = internet); देशभक्तिगीतम् = देशभक्तेः गीतम् (patriotic song); दैनिकपत्रम् (daily paper); सम्भाषणशिबिरम् (conversation camp). Recognising the parts of a compound unlocks its meaning.

(C) नूतनशब्दाः (neologisms — new coinages): A living language must name new things. Modern Sanskrit has coined: सङ्गणकः = computer; दूरदर्शनम् = television; दूरवाणी / दूरभाषः = telephone; चलदूरवाणी = mobile phone; अन्तर्जालम् = internet; सङ्केतस्थलम् = website; वायुयानम् = aeroplane; विद्युत् = electricity. These words are built from classical roots by the ordinary rules of grammar — proof that Panini's system can generate vocabulary for the computer age.

(D) विभक्तिः in modern sentences: सुधर्मा मैसूरुनगरात् प्रकाश्यते (पञ्चमी 'from Mysuru'); छात्रः सङ्गणकेन लिखति (तृतीया 'with a computer'); आकाशवाण्यां वार्ताः श्रूयन्ते (सप्तमी 'on the radio'); कविः देशस्य गीतं रचयति (षष्ठी 'of the country'). The old case-system serves new sentences perfectly.

SUMMARY (सारांशः)

समसामयिकं संस्कृतसाहित्यम् is the Sanskrit literature of our own time. The classical genres — महाकाव्य, खण्डकाव्य, गीतकाव्य, नाटक, कथा — continue unbroken, joined by newer forms: the novel (उपन्यासः), the short story (लघुकथा), the radio play (श्रव्यनाटकम्) and journalism (पत्रकारिता). Sudharma, a Sanskrit daily from Mysuru since 1970, radio and television news, magazines and internet sites carry Sanskrit into daily life. The Sahitya Akademi, whose awards have existed since 1956, honours modern Sanskrit writers; Samskrita Bharati teaches spoken Sanskrit; villages like Mattur speak it. New words — सङ्गणकः, दूरदर्शनम्, अन्तर्जालम् — show the language growing. Sanskrit is thus a जीवद्भाषा, and every student can join its living stream by reading, listening, speaking, writing and performing in Sanskrit.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — समसामयिकं संस्कृतसाहित्यम् (NIOS Sanskrit 309, Chapter 26)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Write Sanskrit words in Devanagari and give explanations in English. Refer to the lesson where needed.

questions.question: What does समसामयिकं संस्कृतसाहित्यम् mean? Give two pieces of evidence from the lesson that Sanskrit is a living language.
questions.answer: समसामयिकम् means 'contemporary, of the present time', so समसामयिकं संस्कृतसाहित्यम् is the Sanskrit literature being composed today. Evidence: (1) new poems, plays, novels and short stories are still written in Sanskrit; (2) Sanskrit journalism exists — e.g. Sudharma, a Sanskrit daily from Mysuru since 1970, and Sanskrit news bulletins on radio.
questions.explanation: Definition of समसामयिक plus any two evidences (literature, journalism, spoken Sanskrit, awards).

questions.question: Give the English meaning of each genre term: गीतकाव्यम्, उपन्यासः, लघुकथा, श्रव्यनाटकम्, पत्रकारिता.
questions.answer: गीतकाव्यम् = lyric poetry / song; उपन्यासः = novel; लघुकथा = short story; श्रव्यनाटकम् = audio play / radio play; पत्रकारिता = journalism.
questions.explanation: The main genre vocabulary of contemporary Sanskrit literature.

questions.question: Write a short note on सुधर्मा (Sudharma).
questions.answer: Sudharma is a Sanskrit daily newspaper (दैनिकपत्रम्) published from Mysuru (Mysore) in Karnataka since 1970. For more than fifty years it has reported news — politics, sport, science, world events — entirely in Sanskrit, making it the best-known example of Sanskrit journalism and strong proof that Sanskrit is a living language.
questions.explanation: Identify: Sanskrit daily, Mysuru, since 1970, reports modern news in Sanskrit.

questions.question: Name four modern Sanskrit coinages (नूतनशब्दाः) with their English meanings.
questions.answer: सङ्गणकः = computer; दूरदर्शनम् = television; दूरवाणी = telephone; अन्तर्जालम् = internet. (Also acceptable: चलदूरवाणी = mobile phone; सङ्केतस्थलम् = website; वायुयानम् = aeroplane.)
questions.explanation: Any four neologisms from the chapter with correct meanings.

questions.question: Explain the compound (समास) meaning of दूरदर्शनम् and अन्तर्जालम्.
questions.answer: दूरदर्शनम् = दूरात् दर्शनम्, 'seeing from afar' — hence television. अन्तर्जालम् = अन्तः जालम्, 'the inner/inter net' — hence the internet. Both are compounds built from classical roots by ordinary grammar to name modern inventions.
questions.explanation: Split each compound into its parts and connect the literal sense to the modern meaning.

questions.question: 'संस्कृतं मृतभाषा नास्ति' (Sanskrit is not a dead language). Justify this statement with evidence from poetry, fiction, drama, journalism and institutions.
questions.answer: Sanskrit is a living language because new literature is continuously composed in it. Poetry: modern गीतकाव्य — patriotic, devotional and social songs — is written and sung today, and even full महाकाव्यs are still composed by contemporary scholar-poets such as Jagadguru Rambhadracharya. Fiction: modern writers produce novels (उपन्यासाः) and short stories (लघुकथाः) about today's life — farmers, students, social questions — in simple prose. Drama: new plays on contemporary themes are staged in schools and universities, and radio plays (श्रव्यनाटकानि) are broadcast. Journalism: Sudharma, a Sanskrit daily from Mysuru since 1970, Sanskrit magazines, radio news bulletins on आकाशवाणी, television news and internet sites report today's news in Sanskrit. Institutions: the Sahitya Akademi's awards (existing since 1956) honour modern Sanskrit writers; Samskrita Bharati teaches lakhs to speak Sanskrit; in Mattur village Sanskrit is a daily spoken tongue. New coinages like सङ्गणकः and अन्तर्जालम् show the vocabulary growing. A language that writes, speaks, reports and grows is alive.
questions.explanation: Marshal evidence across all five areas: poetry, fiction, drama, journalism, institutions/spoken Sanskrit.

questions.question: Describe Sanskrit journalism today: newspaper, magazines, radio, television and internet. Why does journalism keep a language alive?
questions.answer: The flagship of Sanskrit journalism is सुधर्मा (Sudharma), a daily newspaper published from Mysuru since 1970, which reports politics, sport, science and world news entirely in Sanskrit. Several Sanskrit magazines and journals (पत्रिकाः) appear from different parts of India, carrying poems, stories, essays and news. आकाशवाणी (All India Radio) broadcasts daily Sanskrit news bulletins, and दूरदर्शनम् (Doordarshan) has telecast Sanskrit news. On the internet there are Sanskrit websites, blogs, e-magazines and video channels. Journalism keeps a language alive because it forces daily use of the language for new subjects: to report a cricket match or a space launch, journalists must coin and circulate new words (सङ्गणकः, अन्तर्जालम्), keep the style simple and current, and give readers fresh Sanskrit to read every single day.
questions.explanation: Cover all five media and explain the language-renewing effect of daily reporting.

questions.question: How does modern Sanskrit कथासाहित्य (fiction) continue the ancient story tradition, and how does it differ from it?
questions.answer: Continuity: like the पञ्चतन्त्रम् and हितोपदेशः, modern Sanskrit fiction tells stories in prose to delight and instruct readers. Difference: the modern forms are the उपन्यासः (novel) and लघुकथा (short story); their characters are ordinary contemporary people — farmers, students, mothers — their themes are today's social questions, and their style is simple Sanskrit close to speech rather than ornate classical prose.
questions.explanation: One point of continuity (prose storytelling tradition) and clear modern differences (form, theme, style).

questions.question: What is the Sahitya Akademi, and how do its awards help modern Sanskrit literature?
questions.answer: The Sahitya Akademi is India's national academy of letters. Its annual awards for outstanding literary works have existed since 1956, and Sanskrit is among the languages honoured. By giving national recognition and prestige to modern Sanskrit poets and prose writers, the awards encourage authors to keep composing new works in Sanskrit and bring public attention to contemporary Sanskrit writing.
questions.explanation: Identify the Akademi, the since-1956 awards, and their encouraging effect on new writing.

questions.question: Suggest four practical ways a senior-secondary student can engage with living Sanskrit.
questions.answer: Any four: (1) पठनम् — read a Sanskrit magazine or a page of the daily Sudharma; (2) श्रवणम् — listen to the Sanskrit news bulletin on radio or Sanskrit videos on the internet; (3) सम्भाषणम् — attend a spoken-Sanskrit camp (सम्भाषणशिबिरम्) and practise simple sentences daily; (4) लेखनम् — keep a short Sanskrit diary or write small verses; (5) अभिनयः — act in a Sanskrit play on संस्कृतदिनम्; (6) take part in recitation, quiz and essay competitions.
questions.explanation: Any four concrete activities across reading, listening, speaking, writing, performing.

questions.explanation: Both are long-vowel (दीर्घ) sandhis; splitting them is सन्धि-विच्छेद.

questions.question: Name four genres of contemporary Sanskrit literature with the English meaning of each term.
questions.answer: Any four: गीतकाव्यम् = lyric poetry/song; महाकाव्यम् = epic poem; नाटकम् = drama; उपन्यासः = novel; लघुकथा = short story; पत्रकारिता = journalism; निबन्धः = essay.
questions.explanation: Any four correct genre-term pairs earn full marks.

questions.question: Distinguish between उपन्यासः and लघुकथा.
questions.answer: Both are modern prose-fiction forms. The उपन्यासः (novel) is a LONG narrative with many characters and events, published as a full book. The लघुकथा (short story) is a SHORT narrative, usually about one incident or character, often first printed in a Sanskrit magazine (पत्रिका).
questions.explanation: Length and scope distinguish the novel from the short story.

questions.question: List three themes commonly treated in modern Sanskrit poetry.
questions.answer: Any three: love of the nation (देशभक्तिः) and the freedom struggle; nature and the environment (प्रकृतिः); devotion (भक्तिः); social reform and social life; science and modern inventions; the seasons.
questions.explanation: Modern गीतकाव्य ranges from patriotism to science.

questions.question: Who was V. Raghavan, as presented in this lesson?
questions.answer: V. Raghavan of Madras was an eminent twentieth-century Sanskrit scholar and writer. He not only studied classical Sanskrit literature deeply but also wrote and actively promoted NEW Sanskrit compositions, including plays and songs, showing by example that Sanskrit can carry modern thought.
questions.explanation: Scholar + promoter of new Sanskrit writing in the 20th century.

questions.question: How does the महाकाव्य tradition continue in the present day? Illustrate with the example given in the lesson.
questions.answer: The महाकाव्य — a long epic poem in many cantos (सर्गाः) on the life of a great person — is still being composed in the 20th and 21st centuries. The lesson cites the contemporary scholar-poet Jagadguru Rambhadracharya, who has composed modern Sanskrit mahakavyas in recent decades. This shows that the art of Valmiki and Kalidasa is a continuing practice, not a closed chapter of history.
questions.explanation: Define the genre, note its modern continuation, and name the contemporary example.

questions.question: Describe two features of modern Sanskrit short stories.
questions.answer: Any two: (1) they depict ordinary contemporary people — farmers, students, mothers — and social themes such as honesty and poverty; (2) their language is deliberately simple and close to spoken Sanskrit; (3) they are usually first published in Sanskrit magazines; (4) they continue the ancient prose story tradition in a modern form.
questions.explanation: Contemporary subjects and simple style are the key features.

questions.question: In what ways does modern Sanskrit कथासाहित्य both continue and differ from the ancient story tradition of the पञ्चतन्त्र?
questions.answer: Continuity: like the पञ्चतन्त्रम् and हितोपदेशः, modern fiction tells prose stories that entertain and quietly instruct. Difference: the forms are new (उपन्यासः the novel, लघुकथा the short story); the characters are ordinary people of today rather than talking animals and kings; the settings and themes are contemporary — village life, examinations, social problems; and the style is plain modern Sanskrit rather than ornate classical prose.
questions.explanation: One clear continuity plus two or more clear differences.

questions.question: Why is drama considered especially effective for keeping Sanskrit alive?
questions.answer: Because drama makes Sanskrit AUDIBLE and SPOKEN. When students rehearse and perform a play, they speak living Sanskrit dialogue (संवादः), and the audience hears the language used naturally. This takes Sanskrit off the page and onto the tongue and ear, which reading alone cannot do.
questions.explanation: The key idea: drama = heard, spoken Sanskrit.

questions.question: What is a श्रव्यनाटकम्? Where is it presented?
questions.answer: A श्रव्यनाटकम् is an audio play or radio play — a drama meant to be HEARD rather than seen. It is a modern dramatic form broadcast on the radio (आकाशवाणी, All India Radio).
questions.explanation: श्रव्य = to be heard; the radio created this form.

questions.question: What themes do modern Sanskrit plays commonly treat, and what style of language do they use for school performance?
questions.answer: Modern Sanskrit plays treat contemporary themes — social problems, national heroes, school life, and even humorous sketches about modern gadgets. For school and festival performance they use simple, conversational Sanskrit so that student actors can deliver the dialogue and audiences can follow it.
questions.explanation: Contemporary themes + simple conversational style.

questions.question: Write a short note on सुधर्मा (Sudharma).
questions.answer: Sudharma is a Sanskrit daily newspaper (दैनिकपत्रम्) published from Mysuru (Mysore), Karnataka, since 1970. For over fifty years it has reported politics, sport, science and world news entirely in Sanskrit, making it the flagship of Sanskrit journalism and living proof that Sanskrit can serve as a newspaper language.
questions.explanation: Daily + Sanskrit + Mysuru + since 1970 + reports modern news.

questions.question: Describe the role of radio and television in Sanskrit journalism.
questions.answer: आकाशवाणी (All India Radio) broadcasts daily Sanskrit news bulletins, bringing spoken Sanskrit news to listeners across the country, and has also aired Sanskrit radio plays. दूरदर्शनम् (Doordarshan television) has telecast Sanskrit news as well. Together they carry Sanskrit beyond print into the spoken broadcast media.
questions.explanation: AIR bulletins + Doordarshan news = broadcast Sanskrit.

questions.question: Why is journalism considered the most striking proof that Sanskrit is alive? Give two reasons.
questions.answer: (1) A newspaper must describe TODAY's events — politics, sport, science, disasters — every single day; that Sudharma has done this in Sanskrit since 1970 proves the language can express the entire modern world. (2) Daily reporting forces journalists to coin and circulate new words (e.g. सङ्गणकः, अन्तर्जालम्), continuously renewing the vocabulary. A language that reports the present and grows new words daily is unmistakably alive.
questions.explanation: Daily coverage of modern events + constant coining of new vocabulary.

questions.question: What is the Sahitya Akademi, and since when have its awards existed? How do they help Sanskrit?
questions.answer: The Sahitya Akademi is India's national academy of letters. Its annual awards for outstanding literary works have existed since 1956, and Sanskrit is among the languages honoured. The awards help Sanskrit by giving national recognition and prestige to modern Sanskrit writers, which encourages new composition and draws public attention to contemporary Sanskrit literature.
questions.explanation: Academy of letters + since 1956 + recognition encourages new writing.

questions.question: Evaluate the contribution of संस्कृतभारती (Samskrita Bharati) to living Sanskrit.
questions.answer: Samskrita Bharati has made Sanskrit a SPOKEN language for lakhs of people by conducting thousands of सम्भाषणशिबिराणि (spoken-Sanskrit camps) across India and abroad. Its method — simple sentences, everyday vocabulary, conversation from day one — removes the fear that Sanskrit is only for scholars. By turning readers into speakers, it complements literature and journalism: books keep Sanskrit written, but Samskrita Bharati keeps it on people's tongues, which is the surest sign of a living language.
questions.explanation: Camps + simple spoken method + mass reach + complements written Sanskrit.

questions.question: Suggest three practical ways a student can engage with living Sanskrit, using the Sanskrit terms from the lesson.
questions.answer: Any three: पठनम् — read a Sanskrit magazine or a page of Sudharma; श्रवणम् — listen to the Sanskrit news on आकाशवाणी or Sanskrit videos on the अन्तर्जालम्; सम्भाषणम् — attend a सम्भाषणशिबिरम् and practise simple sentences daily; लेखनम् — keep a short Sanskrit diary; अभिनयः — act in a Sanskrit play on संस्कृतदिनम्; enter recitation and essay competitions.
questions.explanation: Any three concrete activities with the Sanskrit terms.

questions.question: Give the Sanskrit coinages for computer, television, internet and telephone. Why does a living language need such new coinages?
questions.answer: Computer = सङ्गणकः; television = दूरदर्शनम्; internet = अन्तर्जालम्; telephone = दूरवाणी (also दूरभाषः). A living language must NAME the new things of its age; by coining such words from classical roots through regular grammar, Sanskrit remains able to discuss modern life — from news to science — in its own vocabulary.
questions.explanation: Four coinages + the need to name new realities.

questions.question: Explain the समास (compound) structure of दूरदर्शनम् and दैनिकपत्रम्.
questions.answer: दूरदर्शनम् = दूरात् दर्शनम्, 'seeing from afar', hence television — a compound joining दूर (far) and दर्शन (seeing). दैनिकपत्रम् = a daily (दैनिक) paper (पत्रम्), hence daily newspaper. Recognising the parts of such समस्तपदानि unlocks the meaning of modern coinages.
questions.explanation: Split each compound and connect literal parts to modern meaning.

questions.question: What is संस्कृतदिनम्, and what activities are held in schools around it?
questions.answer: संस्कृतदिनम् (Sanskrit Day) is celebrated every year on श्रावणपूर्णिमा, the full-moon day of Shravana, and the week around it is observed as Sanskrit Week. Schools and colleges hold recitation of verses, short Sanskrit plays, song performances, and quiz and essay competitions in Sanskrit.
questions.explanation: Shravana Purnima + Sanskrit Week + recitation, drama, competitions.

questions.question: 'संस्कृतं जीवद्भाषा अस्ति' — Sanskrit is a living language. Justify this statement with evidence from at least four different fields discussed in the chapter.
questions.answer: Sanskrit is a living language because it is still used to create, to inform and to converse. (1) Literature: new poems, songs, plays, novels and short stories are continuously composed; even full mahakavyas have been written in the 20th–21st centuries by contemporary scholar-poets such as Jagadguru Rambhadracharya. (2) Journalism: Sudharma, a Sanskrit daily from Mysuru since 1970, along with Sanskrit magazines, reports modern news; आकाशवाणी broadcasts daily Sanskrit bulletins and Doordarshan has telecast Sanskrit news. (3) Speech: Samskrita Bharati's सम्भाषणशिबिराणि have taught lakhs to converse, and in Mattur village Sanskrit is spoken daily. (4) Vocabulary growth: new coinages — सङ्गणकः (computer), दूरदर्शनम् (television), अन्तर्जालम् (internet) — are generated by Paninian grammar, proving the word-making machinery still works. (5) Institutional life: the Sahitya Akademi's awards, existing since 1956, honour modern Sanskrit writers, and Sanskrit Day is celebrated nationwide. A language that writes, reports, speaks and grows in this way is by every test alive.
questions.explanation: At least four fields: literature, journalism, spoken use, coinages, institutions.

questions.question: Describe the main genres of contemporary Sanskrit literature, giving the Sanskrit term and character of each.
questions.answer: Contemporary Sanskrit literature spans verse, prose, stage and press. (1) गीतकाव्यम् (lyric poetry): songs for singing — patriotic, devotional, nature and social — the most popular modern form. (2) महाकाव्यम् (epic): long poems in many cantos on great lives, still composed by contemporary poets; खण्डकाव्यम् is its shorter narrative cousin. (3) नाटकम् (drama): plays on contemporary themes in simple conversational Sanskrit, staged at schools and festivals; the श्रव्यनाटकम् (radio play) is a modern audio form. (4) कथासाहित्यम् (fiction): the उपन्यासः (novel) and लघुकथा (short story), portraying today's people and social questions in simple prose. (5) निबन्धादिगद्यम् (essays and other prose) in magazines. (6) पत्रकारिता (journalism): the daily Sudharma, magazines, radio and TV news and internet media. Together these show every classical genre continuing and new genres flourishing.
questions.explanation: Cover verse (गीत, महाकाव्य), drama, fiction, and journalism with terms.

questions.question: Discuss modern Sanskrit poetry: its forms, themes, and what the continuing mahakavya tradition tells us about the language.
questions.answer: Forms: the commonest form is गीतकाव्यम् — songs with refrains meant for singing in schools, camps and functions — alongside verses in classical metres such as अनुष्टुभ्, and at the grandest scale the महाकाव्यम्, the epic in many सर्गाः. Themes: modern poets sing of the nation and the freedom struggle (देशभक्तिगीतानि), of nature and the environment, of devotion, of social reform, and even of science and modern life — the subjects of their own age. The continuing mahakavya tradition — with contemporary scholar-poets such as Jagadguru Rambhadracharya composing full epics, and twentieth-century scholars like V. Raghavan promoting new composition — tells us two things: first, that the highest classical art-forms are still practised, not merely studied; and second, that Sanskrit's poetic machinery (metre, figures, grammar) remains fully productive. A language in which new epics are born is not a museum language but a living medium of imagination.
questions.explanation: Forms (गीत, metres, महाकाव्य) + modern themes + significance of continuity.

questions.question: Write an essay on modern Sanskrit कथासाहित्य (fiction): its roots, forms, themes, style and importance.
questions.answer: Roots: Sanskrit possesses one of the world's oldest and most influential story traditions — the पञ्चतन्त्रम् and हितोपदेशः travelled the globe in translation. Forms: modern writers carry this tradition into the उपन्यासः (novel), a long book-length narrative, and the लघुकथा (short story), usually first printed in Sanskrit magazines (पत्रिकाः). Themes: contemporary life — a farmer anxious about the rains, a student before an examination, a village mother — and social questions of honesty, poverty and kindness. Style: deliberately simple Sanskrit (सरला भाषा), close to speech, so ordinary readers can enjoy it without a commentary. Importance: modern fiction proves that Sanskrit is not confined to verse or religious subjects; its prose can narrate today's secular society in today's settings. Every new story adds evidence that Sanskrit remains a complete literary language, able to do what any modern language does.
questions.explanation: Roots, two forms, contemporary themes, simple style, significance.

questions.question: Analyse the place of drama in the modern Sanskrit movement. How can schools use Sanskrit drama, and what is the role of the श्रव्यनाटकम्?
questions.answer: Drama holds a special place because it makes Sanskrit a HEARD and SPOKEN language. Modern playwrights, continuing the tradition of Bhasa and Kalidasa, write short plays on contemporary themes — social problems, national heroes, school life, humorous sketches — in simple conversational Sanskrit. Schools can use drama powerfully: students who rehearse a play internalise pronunciation, vocabulary and sentence patterns through dialogue (संवादः); performances on संस्कृतदिनम्, at annual functions and youth festivals let whole audiences hear living Sanskrit; and preparing costumes, narration and songs draws even non-actors into the language. The श्रव्यनाटकम् (radio play), broadcast on आकाशवाणी, extends drama beyond the stage: it reaches listeners everywhere, depends purely on spoken Sanskrit, and trains the ear. Thus drama, staged and broadcast, converts Sanskrit from a subject to be read into a language to be lived.
questions.explanation: Why drama matters (spoken Sanskrit), school uses, and the radio play's reach.

questions.question: Give a full account of Sanskrit journalism today — print, radio, television and internet — and assess its contribution to the life of the language.
questions.answer: Print: the flagship is सुधर्मा (Sudharma), a Sanskrit daily newspaper published from Mysuru since 1970, reporting politics, sport, science and world news entirely in Sanskrit for over half a century; many Sanskrit magazines and journals (पत्रिकाः) across India carry poems, stories, essays and news. Radio: आकाशवाणी broadcasts daily Sanskrit news bulletins and has aired Sanskrit radio plays. Television: दूरदर्शनम् has telecast Sanskrit news. Internet: Sanskrit websites, blogs, e-magazines and video channels are multiplying. Contribution: journalism gives Sanskrit a DAILY life — readers receive fresh Sanskrit every morning; reporting modern events forces the constant coining of new words (सङ्गणकः, अन्तर्जालम्), keeping vocabulary current; the simple newspaper style creates an accessible modern prose; and the very existence of a Sanskrit daily is public proof, renewed each day, that the language lives. Journalism is thus both a product and an engine of living Sanskrit.
questions.explanation: All four media with facts, then assessment: daily use, new words, accessible prose, public proof.

questions.question: Evaluate the role of institutions and awards in nurturing contemporary Sanskrit literature.
questions.answer: Institutions provide the soil in which modern Sanskrit grows. (1) The साहित्य-अकादमी (Sahitya Akademi), India's national academy of letters, has given annual awards since 1956; by honouring outstanding Sanskrit works it confers national recognition and prestige, motivating authors and signalling to the public that Sanskrit writing is a living art. (2) Sanskrit universities and academies teach composition, publish new books and journals, and give their own prizes, creating both writers and readers. (3) संस्कृतभारती (Samskrita Bharati) attacks the problem from the spoken side: its सम्भाषणशिबिराणि have taught lakhs to converse, building the audience without which literature starves. (4) Government recognition — Sanskrit's place among the 22 Eighth-Schedule languages and the celebration of Sanskrit Day/Week — keeps the language in public life and in schools. Evaluation: no single institution suffices; awards create prestige, universities create competence, camps create speakers, and state recognition creates space. Working together they have kept a continuous stream of new Sanskrit writing flowing into the twenty-first century.
questions.explanation: Akademi since 1956, universities, Samskrita Bharati, state recognition — with an overall judgement.

questions.question: Design a one-month 'Living Sanskrit' plan for yourself as a senior-secondary student. Include reading, listening, speaking, writing and performing activities, and use at least four modern Sanskrit coinages in your plan.
questions.answer: Sample plan. Week 1 — पठनम्: read one page of the daily Sudharma or a Sanskrit magazine each evening; note five new words daily in a notebook. Week 2 — श्रवणम्: listen to the आकाशवाणी Sanskrit news bulletin every morning; watch one Sanskrit video on the अन्तर्जालम् (internet) using my सङ्गणकः (computer) or चलदूरवाणी (mobile phone) each weekend. Week 3 — सम्भाषणम् and लेखनम्: attend a सम्भाषणशिबिरम् or practise ten simple spoken sentences daily with a friend (भवान् कथम् अस्ति?); begin a five-line Sanskrit diary each night; write one letter in simple Sanskrit. Week 4 — अभिनयः and प्रदर्शनम्: rehearse a ten-minute Sanskrit play with classmates for संस्कृतदिनम्; enter the school recitation or essay competition; on दूरदर्शनम् or online, watch a Sanskrit news clip and retell it aloud in three Sanskrit sentences. Review: at month-end, count new words learnt, diary pages written and sentences spoken — then repeat with harder material. This plan touches all five doors — reading, listening, speaking, writing, performing — through which a student enters living Sanskrit.
questions.explanation: A structured, personal, multi-skill plan using coinages like सङ्गणकः, अन्तर्जालम्, चलदूरवाणी, दूरदर्शनम्.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer:
'Every morning, a thin newspaper printed entirely in Devanagari Sanskrit reaches subscribers by post and email. It has been published from a city in Karnataka since 1970, and its pages report elections, cricket scores and space missions — all in Sanskrit.'
(a) Name this newspaper and its city. (b) What kind of publication is it (Sanskrit term)? (c) What does its existence prove about Sanskrit?
questions.answer: (a) The newspaper is सुधर्मा (Sudharma), published from Mysuru (Mysore), Karnataka. (b) It is a दैनिकपत्रम् — a daily newspaper. (c) Its existence proves that Sanskrit is a living language capable of reporting the modern world — politics, sport and science — every single day, and that Sanskrit journalism (पत्रकारिता) is a working reality, not a dream.
questions.explanation: Sudharma + Mysuru + दैनिकपत्रम् + proof of living Sanskrit.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer:
'During the summer holidays, Ananya attended a ten-day camp where, from the first morning, everyone spoke only simple Sanskrit — भवती कथम् अस्ति? इदं पुस्तकम् अस्ति। By the last day she could describe her home and school in Sanskrit sentences.'
(a) What is such a camp called in Sanskrit? (b) Which organisation mentioned in the lesson is famous for conducting such camps? (c) Which skill (Sanskrit term) did Ananya chiefly develop?
questions.answer: (a) Such a camp is a सम्भाषणशिबिरम् (spoken-Sanskrit / conversation camp). (b) संस्कृतभारती (Samskrita Bharati) is famous for conducting thousands of such camps. (c) She chiefly developed सम्भाषणम् — the skill of speaking (conversation), along with श्रवणम् (listening).
questions.explanation: सम्भाषणशिबिरम् + Samskrita Bharati + speaking skill.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer:
'At a ceremony in Delhi, an elderly Sanskrit poet received a national literary award from India's academy of letters for his recent book of Sanskrit poems. Newspapers reported that such awards have been given since 1956, and young Sanskrit writers said the news encouraged them to keep writing.'
(a) Which institution gave the award? (b) Since when have its awards existed? (c) Evaluate: in what TWO ways do such awards help modern Sanskrit literature?
questions.answer: (a) The साहित्य-अकादमी (Sahitya Akademi), India's national academy of letters. (b) Its annual awards have existed since 1956. (c) Two ways: (1) they give national recognition and prestige to modern Sanskrit writers, motivating them — and younger authors — to keep composing new works; (2) they draw public and media attention to contemporary Sanskrit writing, winning it readers and respect it might otherwise not receive.
questions.explanation: Sahitya Akademi + 1956 + motivation and public attention.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer:
'A contemporary scholar-poet has composed a full Sanskrit epic in many cantos on the life of a great figure, following the classical rules of metre and poetic ornament, yet written in our own century.'
(a) Which genre (Sanskrit term) is this work? (b) What are its divisions called? (c) Name the contemporary scholar-poet mentioned in the lesson as an example. (d) What does such a work prove about the Sanskrit poetic tradition?
questions.answer: (a) The work is a महाकाव्यम् (epic poem). (b) Its divisions are सर्गाः (cantos). (c) The lesson cites Jagadguru Rambhadracharya as a contemporary composer of Sanskrit mahakavyas. (d) It proves that the epic tradition of Valmiki and Kalidasa is still practised — the highest classical art-form remains productive, so Sanskrit poetry is a living, continuing tradition, not merely a subject of study.
questions.explanation: महाकाव्य + सर्गाः + Rambhadracharya + living epic tradition.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer:
'For Sanskrit Week, Class 12 students staged a fifteen-minute Sanskrit play about a village family debating whether to send their daughter to college. The dialogue was simple, and the audience laughed and clapped at the right places, following every word.'
(a) Why did the playwright choose simple conversational Sanskrit? (b) What contemporary feature marks this play's THEME? (c) State two benefits the student actors gained.
questions.answer: (a) Simple conversational Sanskrit lets student actors deliver the lines naturally and lets the audience follow the story — the goal is communication, not display. (b) The theme is contemporary social life — a present-day family question (a daughter's college education) rather than a mythological subject. (c) Benefits: the actors practised speaking and listening to living Sanskrit through dialogue (संवादः), and they gained confidence performing the language publicly (with vocabulary and pronunciation internalised through rehearsal).
questions.explanation: Accessibility + contemporary social theme + spoken-Sanskrit benefits.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer:
'In a recent Sanskrit magazine, a short story described a farmer named Devadatta watching the empty sky for rain, worrying about his loan and his son's school fees, until a neighbour's kindness gives him hope.'
(a) Which genre (Sanskrit term) is this piece? (b) List two features that make it typically MODERN Sanskrit fiction. (c) Which ancient Sanskrit tradition does such storytelling continue?
questions.answer: (a) It is a लघुकथा (short story). (b) Modern features: its hero is an ordinary contemporary person (a farmer with a loan and school fees) and its theme is present-day social and economic life; it appears in a Sanskrit magazine (पत्रिका) and is written in simple, near-spoken prose. (c) It continues Sanskrit's ancient prose story tradition — the line of the पञ्चतन्त्रम् and हितोपदेशः — in a modern form.
questions.explanation: लघुकथा + ordinary characters/contemporary themes/simple style + Panchatantra lineage.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer:
'At 6:55 each morning, Rajan's grandfather turns on the radio. A clear voice reads the day's news — इदानीं संस्कृतवार्ताः श्रूयन्ताम् — covering the parliament, the weather and yesterday's cricket match, all in Sanskrit, in under ten minutes.'
(a) Which broadcaster (Sanskrit name) airs such bulletins? (b) What does वार्ताः mean? (c) Why are such broadcasts important for Sanskrit?
questions.answer: (a) आकाशवाणी (All India Radio) broadcasts the Sanskrit news bulletins. (b) वार्ताः means 'news'. (c) They are important because they bring SPOKEN Sanskrit to listeners across the country every day, prove that Sanskrit can report current affairs — parliament, weather, sport — and give learners a free daily model of clear modern Sanskrit to listen to.
questions.explanation: आकाशवाणी + वार्ताः = news + daily spoken-Sanskrit exposure.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer:
'Visitors to a village on the banks of the Tunga river in Karnataka are surprised to hear shopkeepers, children and farmers conversing in Sanskrit — bargaining, joking and calling out greetings in the ancient tongue as their everyday language.'
(a) Which famous village fits this description? (b) What does this village demonstrate about Sanskrit? (c) Which Sanskrit term from the lesson describes such a language?
questions.answer: (a) Mattur (मत्तूरु) in Karnataka. (b) It demonstrates that Sanskrit can function as an ordinary spoken mother-tongue of daily life — for shopping, joking and greeting — not merely as a book language. (c) Such a language is a जीवद्भाषा — a living language.
questions.explanation: Mattur + everyday spoken Sanskrit + जीवद्भाषा.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer:
'Priya opens her सङ्गणकः, connects to the अन्तर्जालम्, and visits a Sanskrit सङ्केतस्थलम् where she reads an e-magazine, watches a Sanskrit video lesson, and posts a two-line Sanskrit comment from her चलदूरवाणी.'
(a) Give the English meaning of the four Devanagari coinages in the passage. (b) What does Priya's routine show about where living Sanskrit is found today?
questions.answer: (a) सङ्गणकः = computer; अन्तर्जालम् = internet; सङ्केतस्थलम् = website; चलदूरवाणी = mobile phone. (b) Her routine shows that living Sanskrit now thrives in digital media — websites, e-magazines, videos and social comments — so a student can read, hear and even WRITE Sanskrit online daily, using vocabulary the language has coined for the digital age.
questions.explanation: Four coinages + Sanskrit's digital presence.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer:
'The new-arrivals shelf of a Sanskrit library holds: a book of patriotic songs; a two-volume epic in thirty cantos on a saint's life; a collection of twelve stories about city life; a slim playbook for schools; and a bound volume of last year's daily newspaper issues.'
Identify the genre (Sanskrit term) of EACH of the five items, and state what the shelf as a whole shows about contemporary Sanskrit literature.
questions.answer: (1) Book of patriotic songs = गीतकाव्यम् (देशभक्तिगीतानि). (2) Two-volume epic in thirty cantos = महाकाव्यम् (in सर्गाः). (3) Collection of twelve stories = कथासाहित्यम् / लघुकथासङ्ग्रहः (short stories). (4) Playbook for schools = नाटकम् (drama). (5) Bound daily newspaper = पत्रकारिता — a दैनिकपत्रम् like Sudharma. Together the shelf shows that contemporary Sanskrit literature is being produced across ALL genres — lyric, epic, fiction, drama and journalism — proving that the whole literary ecosystem of a living language, classical and modern forms alike, is active in Sanskrit today.
questions.explanation: Five genre identifications + the conclusion: all genres alive simultaneously.
